questions.question: Explain the economic problem and show how the production possibility curve draws it, reading points on, inside and beyond the curve.
questions.expected_answer: The economic problem is scarcity: unlimited wants against limited resources — a permanent condition, not a temporary shortage — which forces choice, and every choice carries an opportunity cost, the value of the next best alternative forgone. The PPC draws this with one product on each axis and a curve bowing outward showing every maximum combination producible with resources fully and efficiently used. A point on the curve is efficient; a point inside shows underutilisation — unemployed workers and idle capacity, as in South Africa with unemployment above thirty percent; a point beyond is unattainable today. The downward slope is opportunity cost — more of one product means giving up some of the other — and the whole curve shifts outward when resources grow or technology improves, which is economic growth.

questions.question: Describe the circular flow with its leakages and injections, and distinguish GDP from GNI with the trap each definition carries.
questions.expected_answer: Households sell factors of production to firms on the factor market and earn income; firms sell goods and services back on the product market — money circulating one way, goods and factors the other. Leakages drain the flow: savings, taxes and imports; injections refill it: investment, government spending and exports. Injections above leakages grow the flow; leakages above injections shrink it. GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced within the borders in a year — final goods only, to avoid double-counting intermediate goods like flour inside bread, and the where-rule means a foreign-owned mine in Limpopo counts. GNI follows the who-rule, adding South Africans' factor income earned abroad and subtracting foreigners' earnings here. Per capita versions allow comparison, but the numbers miss unpaid work, the informal sector, distribution and environmental costs.

questions.question: Use the drought example to show how a market reaches a new equilibrium, distinguishing a movement along a curve from a shift of the curve.
questions.expected_answer: A price change causes a movement along a curve; any other factor — income, tastes, related prices, costs, technology, weather — shifts the whole curve. A drought shifts maize supply left: at every price less is offered. At the old price quantity demanded now exceeds quantity supplied — excess demand — and the shortage bids the price up. The market moves along the demand curve to a new equilibrium at a higher price and lower quantity. The four-step method for any shock: name the curve that shifts, the direction, the excess at the old price, and the new equilibrium. Equilibrium itself is the single price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied — no queue, no pile — found in a table at the row where the two quantity columns are equal.
